summary: ORBIT is an offline health companion for astronauts on long missions. On the way to Mars, Earth is 3 to 22 minutes away, so the astronaut has to notice health changes first, with little time and little medical training. ORBIT keeps the screen simple and the reading precise: it compares body, mind and crew life with her own baseline instead of Earth averages, and raises an early cross-domain signal when two domains stay yellow for two days, before small changes become problems. She then picks up to two evidence-based protective actions; ORBIT asks "Did it help?" and learns what works for her, while a care tank makes her protective habits visible. Body status always reaches the crew medical officer; mind and crew data leave the device only if she chooses, at the pace the communication delay allows. Every threshold shows its rule and its source. ORBIT uses NASA data (Human Research Program risks, DONKI space weather, MSL RAD dose, EPIC images of Earth and planetary fact sheets) and runs on synthetic data. It supports decisions; it does not diagnose.
details:
ORBIT: Catch the early signals. Act onboard.

Live app (public, no sign-in, works offline after the first visit): https://carlosjcd.github.io/orbit/

Code and documentation: https://github.com/CarlosJCD/orbit


WHAT IT DOES

On a Mars mission, Earth is 3 to 22 minutes away, one way. Astronauts sleep about six hours a night in flight, problems tend to arrive together, and even Earth's normal values mislead in space. The astronaut has to notice changes first, with little time and little medical training. ORBIT is an offline health companion that keeps the screen simple and the reading precise. It reads body, mind and crew life against each astronaut's own baseline, raises an early signal before small changes become problems, helps her choose protective actions, learns which ones help her, and sends the right information to the right person at the pace the delay allows. ORBIT supports decisions; it does not diagnose. The demo runs on synthetic data.

HOW IT WORKS: THE ORBIT CYCLE

- Observe: a one-minute daily check-in; sleep, heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, glucose and exercise; a 3-minute PVT-B-style alertness task; weekly PHQ-2 and GAD-2 screens; crew climate; contact with home; and symptoms or pain drawn on a body map.

- Read: every value is compared with her own 14-day baseline, not with Earth norms. When two of the three domains (Body, Mind, Crew) stay yellow for two days in a row, ORBIT raises an early cross-domain signal.

- Boost: a safety question first, then up to four evidence-based actions; she picks up to two (for example, protecting tonight's sleep window or sending a message home). The app explains "Why only 2?".

- Iterate: "Did it help?" right after and the next day; her answers reorder future suggestions.

- Transmit: body status always reaches the crew medical officer; mind and crew data leave only if she switches them on. The delay to Earth is drawn as a path.

The demo follows a fictional astronaut, Lena, on days 23 to 30 of a Mars transit. On day 23, 38.0 °C is her normal in flight, so there is no alarm. On day 25, one short night brings one tip and no alarm. On day 26, all three domains turn yellow, but one day is not enough. On day 27, the same pattern repeats and ORBIT raises an early signal before any symptom. She chooses two actions, answers "Did it help?", and by day 30 she is back in her range.

SIX VALUE PROPOSITIONS, AND WHY

1. Simple on top, precise underneath. Home is her body: one figure, one state, one next step. Every card opens "Why?" with her baseline, the rule, the NASA risk and the source. A tired person should face few options at once; working memory holds about four items.

2. Body, mind and crew in one view. Health is biological, psychological and social at once (the biopsychosocial model), and NASA counts isolation and distance from Earth among the five hazards of spaceflight.

3. Signals before symptoms. Personal baselines avoid false alarms from Earth norms (core temperature runs about 1 °C higher in long flights), and convergence across domains reflects how problems travel together (short sleep comes with slower reactions and more stress on the ISS).

4. Protective factors, not just risks. A care tank counts what keeps her well (check-ins, care actions, alertness sessions, calm games). It only fills: no points, no ranking, nothing taken away.

5. Feedback that learns. Choosing raises motivation, but many plans at once lower commitment, so she picks up to two actions; "Did it help?" turns each choice into personal evidence (just-in-time adaptive intervention design).

6. Onboard and private by design. Built for the communication delay; check-in answers, the private journal and games never leave the device; no account; works offline.

INTENDED IMPACT

ORBIT helps astronauts and crew medical officers act earlier during Earth-independent operations, when help from Earth cannot be instant. A next step is to test it with analog crews (HERA, Antarctic stations). Use with isolated and confined workers on Earth is a hypothesis we have not tested.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

- A cross-domain convergence rule instead of single-metric alarms.

- A protective-factors tank that never empties, instead of points or streaks.

- Choice that is limited on purpose, with the reason explained inside the app.

- NASA data the astronaut can feel: Constellations, a calm puzzle built on NASA planetary fact sheets with no timer and no score; Earth Window, a NASA EPIC photo of Earth; live DONKI space weather plus a replay of the May 2024 solar particle events.

- Color, shape and word for every state (green circle, yellow triangle, red square), so it reads at a glance and works for color-blind users.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Safety: red physical states go to the crew medical officer; a red mental state is hers to trigger ("I want to talk to someone today"); alarm-sign symptom buttons go straight to a person; no diagnostic language.

- False alarms versus missed drifts: in our simulation of healthy crews, early signals averaged 1.3 per mission; weekly screens, a 14-day contact trend and a direct talk button cover slow drifts.

- Privacy: medical communication follows NASA-STD-3001; data stay on the device.

- Accessibility and context: dark "Mission" theme for the cabin, light "Day" theme for projectors, English and Spanish.

- Honesty: synthetic data; not yet reviewed by a physician; thresholds without a source say "team criterion" in the app; the alertness task follows the format of the ISS Reaction Self-Test (PVT-B), but our web version is not validated.

TOOLS

React, TypeScript, Vite, a service worker for offline use, Vitest (153 automated tests, including the full demo story), oxlint, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages (daily refresh of NASA DONKI data). Evidence: a knowledge base of 52 sources behind 134 parameters, and a 32-paper psychology evidence matrix. SI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) is declared in the README.

TEAM

Four people across engineering, data and psychology.
